abstract: Coding agents can destroy data, leak secrets and message the wrong person faster than a human can review. Could a decision model catch these risks at runtime? We evaluated 22 hosted decision models and two prompted general models as classifiers for a multi-rule policy engine. A synthetic dataset of 2,643 tool calls was labeled blind against 28 rules, with a sealed holdout. With a single shared preamble in both conditions, explicit boundaries written as examples and counterexamples raised recall by 5.5–26.1 percentage points on all 23 available models and reduced false positives on 21. Jev 1.14’s recall rose from 89.3% to 98.2%, while unnecessary interruptions fell from 30.6% to 4.8% of 252 clean actions. With examples, its median latency was 120 ms at \$0.46 per thousand requests. Strong models retained the recall gains when concrete names were replaced by generic descriptions; three largely retained them when the same boundaries were written as prose. On 16 new scenarios written after the initial studies, a follow-up improved recall on 22 of 23 models and reduced unnecessary interruptions on 21. We release the dataset, rule texts and harness.

sections.body: The paper asks whether hosted decision models can judge a coding agent's proposed tool calls against several policy rules at runtime. The authors tested 22 hosted decision models and two prompted general models on a synthetic dataset of 2,643 tool calls labeled against 28 rules. Four hypotheses covered one request per call within a 3-second deadline and at most 0.50 USD per thousand requests, definitions alone, added examples, and removing concrete names. The introduction reports that explicit boundaries improved detection and reduced interruptions, while a one-sentence definition alone was not enough.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: The paper asks whether hosted decision models can judge a coding agent's proposed tool calls against several policy rules at runtime.

sections.body: Decision models are new, and related work shows that model choice depends on the task. A trained classifier can outperform decision models when labeled task data exist. Other studies report wording sensitivity and confidently missed attack categories. Permission-gate and runtime-check work measures action-level false blocks, and Llama Guard uses policy descriptions and examples. The authors say their contribution is a comparison across providers and rule texts in a multi-rule coding-agent gate. They do not establish calibration or resistance to adversarial inputs.
sections.heading: Prior Literature
sections.headline: Prior evaluations show model choice depends on the task, and this paper adds per-rule errors with action-level interruption measures.

sections.body: Because user tool calls are private, the authors built a synthetic dataset of 2,643 tool calls grouped into 106 families of 18–32 cases each. Cases include positives, hard negatives, undecidable cases and injections. Each case is scored tool-only, the setting used for headline numbers, or with trusted project context. Claude Opus 5.5 relabeled every case blind under a written rulebook. The two agreed on 99.9% of labels and 96.6% of whole cases before adjudication. The holdout has 1,108 cases in 44 families and 1,610 deny-side positives, sealed by hash before inference. A confirmation set of 16 scenarios and 320 cases was built later.
sections.heading: Data
sections.headline: A synthetic set of 2,643 tool calls was labeled blind against 28 rules, with a sealed holdout of 1,108 cases.

sections.body: The study evaluated 22 hosted decision models from 15 vendors and two prompted general models, Gemini 3.1 and 3.5 Flash-Lite. Each run pinned the requested model version and checked the returned identifier. Most models used vendor endpoints or OpenRouter's Decisions endpoint, and OpenAI received equivalent predicate questions. The Gemini models received the same rule text and a JSON schema requesting one probability per rule. SubQ Snap and Nace Drex v2.0 allow at most 16 questions, so their 27 questions were split into two parallel requests and merged. Perplexity Decider v1.1 was retired, leaving 23 models for the placement and confirmation studies.
sections.heading: Models
sections.headline: 22 hosted decision models from 15 vendors and two prompted general models were pinned to exact versions.

sections.body: Tool-only inputs carried 27 rule questions. Policy code made the final decision from per-rule scores at a fixed threshold of 0.5. Each rule has a name and a one-sentence definition under a shared preamble. The examples were written from the definitions without seeing cases or results. Controls removed concrete names or wrote the same boundaries as prose. Metrics were recall, false-positive rate and Youden's J, with 95% confidence intervals from 2,000 bootstrap resamples of whole families. The unnecessary interruption rate counts clean actions with any deny-side score at or above 0.5, and the holdout has 252 clean actions. Across 42 completed runs, the authors made 1.43 million API calls at approximately 944 USD.
sections.heading: Methods
sections.headline: Two language models wrote examples for fixed rule definitions, scored on a sealed holdout with family-level bootstrap intervals.

sections.body: Definitions with a single shared preamble reached 89.3–90.4% recall on the leading models, with false-positive rates of 1.15–2.49%. Opus examples raised recall by 5.5–26.1 points on all 23 models, and seven reached 98.1–98.6%. For Jev 1.14, interruptions on clean actions fell from 77/252 (30.6%) to 12/252 (4.8%). On 16 new families, the follow-up improved recall on 22 of 23 models. Cutting actions over 16 KiB to a prefix lost 9–39 recall points on 19 of 21 tested models, based on 20 holdout actions. Runs spread across dates, so latency and cost comparisons may not reflect the added examples.
sections.heading: Results
sections.headline: Explicit examples raised recall on all 23 models and reduced interruptions for Jev 1.14 from 30.6% to 4.8%.

sections.body: With Opus examples, 19 of 23 available models had a 95th-percentile latency below three seconds. Nine cost at most 0.50 USD per thousand requests, and eight met both targets. Definitions alone detected 85–90% of hazards on the eight leading models but interrupted 12–32% of harmless actions, so the short-definition hypothesis was not supported. Examples improved detection, with the largest gains for models weakest on definitions. Removing concrete names left the ten strongest models within half a point, while six weaker models lost 2–10 points. The product now uses Jev 1.14.0 as primary, SubQ Snap for oversize actions and Perplexity Decider v1.2 as fallback.
sections.heading: Analysis
sections.headline: Explicit boundaries improved detection, while removing concrete names cost strong models little, and eight models met both latency and cost targets.

sections.body: Explicit policy boundaries improved hazard detection and usually reduced false alarms across decision models, and the gains extended to new scenarios. Seven models reached 98% recall with the fuller text, differing in latency and price rather than accuracy. For builders, the authors advise specifying inclusions and exclusions, preserving the evidence each rule needs, and measuring interruptions per action rather than false positives per rule. Open questions include how far the user's request and trusted project context recover misses, whether thresholds other than 0.5 trade recall for fewer interruptions, and how stable hosted models are between runs.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Explicit policy boundaries improved detection and usually reduced false alarms; open questions remain on context and thresholds.

sections.body: All cases are synthetic and cover 28 of 67 rule templates, with none of the agent self-control rules. The dataset skews small, with 75% of cases under 1 KB against a 55% target. Interruption estimates come from 252 clean holdout actions and 60 confirmation actions, so they do not estimate production burden. Labels were generated and adjudicated by models, and human review covered development cases only. The holdout was reused after results were seen, and the confirmation set is small. Identical requests two weeks apart changed recall by 2.5–3.8 points on Celeris-1 and Span-02. Costs use list prices, not invoices.
sections.heading: Limitations
sections.headline: Results rest on synthetic cases, a reused holdout and runs spread over dates, which bound what the numbers show.

sections.body: The authors state that no real person, organization, host, credential or transcript content appears in the dataset. Every identifier comes from a fictional allowlist, and credential-shaped literals are fabricated and fail checksum validation. Shape statistics mined from the maintainer's own transcripts are reported only as aggregate quantiles. Generative models were used to generate and label cases, write the rule texts under test, and assist with analysis and drafting.
sections.heading: Ethical Considerations
sections.headline: The dataset includes no real people, organizations, credentials or transcripts, and generative models produced its cases and labels.

sections.body: Table 2 lists the 24 evaluated models with their provider, access path, identifier and list price per million input tokens, since results describe particular services and dates. Table 3 gives the numerical results behind Figures 1 and 2 for the holdout, including recall, false-positive rate, interruption and miss rates, and latency and cost for the Opus text. Table 4 gives the other rule texts on the same holdout, including the per-rule-preamble definitions and the name-free Opus text. The appendix also points to label rules in Table 5, a complete example case, and unchanged definitions.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists the 24 evaluated models with endpoints and identifiers, plus numerical results and rule texts.
